site.title: Praxis Map
site.lead: An interactive map and statistical analysis of where there is no contracted {doctor} in Hungary — from public NEAK data, refreshed monthly, by county, járás and settlement, with a European comparison. It also shows what goes with the gaps: where more GP districts are vacant, the surgery tends to be farther away, income and education lower, jobseekers more numerous and avoidable mortality higher. That is association, not proven cause.

methodology.heading: Methodology
methodology.p1: The data come from the monthly lists published by the National Health Insurance Fund of Hungary (NEAK): vacant dental and GP services, vacant dental services with terminated contracts, and the registries of contracted providers. NEAK's data are informative in nature and reflect the monthly financing-contract status — they are not real-time operational data.
methodology.p2: A district is “vacant” when it has no contracted physician. This is not the same as “unserved”: residents of vacant districts are usually covered by a substitute physician, which public data does not show. The “terminated contract” category marks dental districts whose financing contract has also ended — NEAK publishes no such list for the GP branch. Persistent vacancy is a legal category: under section 2 (1) b) of Government Decree 313/2011 (XII. 23.) it applies to a district with a territorial obligation that for more than six months can be met only by substitution, or where the municipality cannot arrange care other than substitution for at least six months.
methodology.p3: The denominator of the vacancy rate is the number of unique primary-care district codes (FIN or HSZ) in NEAK's registries. On the dental branch adult, paediatric, mixed and school-youth services count (on-call and university services and specialist care do not); on the GP branch, districts with a territorial care obligation (T) — practices without one (TN) are excluded, as they cannot appear on the vacancy list either.
methodology.p4: Practice coordinates are determined with OpenStreetMap's Nominatim service. Where an address could not be identified precisely, the settlement centre is marked and flagged on the map. District boundaries are not officially published by anyone, so the maps colour counties and járás, and show districts as points at the surgery.
methodology.p5: On the GP branch the settlement search is based on the official list of settlements served by each district, so small villages can also be found; the dental registry only records the practice seat, so there the search covers the practices' settlements and the settlements served by terminated districts.
methodology.p6: The full processing code and every month's raw source file are public in the project repository — every number can be traced back to its original source. The contracted physician's name of a filled practice is shown from NEAK's public contracted-provider database; we never publish a personal name for a vacant or terminated district or for a substitute physician.
methodology.p7: The per-capita indicators (share of population living in a vacant district; districts per 10,000 residents; settlement populations) use the resident population of the HCSO Gazetteer as of 1 January 2025. This single edition is applied to every archived month — for historical months this is an approximation, noted here. Settlements are identified by HCSO code and settlement name; Budapest's districts are counted separately.
methodology.p8: The legal category of long-term vacant districts is taken from the continuously updated lists of the OKFŐ Primary Care Directorate (alapellatas.okfo.gov.hu). The list carries no NEAK code, so matching uses the settlement, the service type and the starting month of the vacancy; the list's as-of date is shown in the interface. The flag applies to the current month and is not applied retroactively to historical months.
methodology.embedText: The map can be embedded in any page with the code below (parameter k: dental or gp; optional parameter m: county name):
methodology.p9: The EESZT supplement (source H) is built from three public registers of the EESZT master-data publication: NEAK_FINSZOLG (financed services), EUSZOLG_PUBLIKUS (healthcare providers) and EUSZOLG_ENGEDELY_PUBLIKUS (operating licences). Matching uses official codes only: from the NEAK FIN code through the organisational-unit code to the licence of the district's own profession (GP 6301–6303, dental 1300/1304/1305). We check whether the licensed premises lie in the district's settlement and whether the licensee's tax number matches the financed provider; differences are flagged, and where a FIN points to several licences at different premises no premises are shown. The district number is extracted from the official service name with a strict pattern. The provider name is shown only for filled districts; for vacant districts no free-text name field is taken over, as organisational-unit names often carry the former physician's name. On the EESZT map each district is drawn at its licensed premises; addresses are geocoded with OpenStreetMap Nominatim (at most 1 request per second, cached). Where an address cannot be resolved at street level, the settlement centre is used — shown as a fainter point on the map and in the "approximate location" column; districts without coordinates are not drawn.

footer.publicOnly: This site works only with publicly released official and statistical data: it downloads them every month, archives them unchanged — the archive is public so the figures can be checked — and analyses them in aggregate. We carry out no data collection of our own: nothing is gathered about visitors or patients, and the site holds no patient or other personal health data.
footer.disclaimer: NEAK states its own data to be informational, published from the monthly financing contract records. The figures here are not a basis for administrative, legal or care-planning decisions.
footer.vacantNotUnserved: A vacant district does not mean there is no care: residents are usually seen by a substitute physician, which the public data does not show. Check opening hours and the place of care with the provider.
footer.names: A physician's name appears only where NEAK itself publishes it: on filled districts in the contracted provider list. Never for vacant or dissolved districts, nor for substitutes.
footer.noPersonal: The site asks for no registration and stores no visitor data in its own systems. Visitor statistics (Google Analytics) and speed measurement (Vercel Speed Insights) start only if you separately consent — without consent no measurement code is loaded and no cookie is set. Your language choice and map layers are kept in your own browser and never reach us. Google Fonts serves the typefaces; MapTiler and OpenStreetMap serve the street map, only if you open it. Details in the privacy notice.

why.heading: Why does primary care matter?
why.lead: The GP, the paediatrician and the dentist are the gateway to healthcare: they are the first to see a complaint, they know the family, the medical history, the everyday life of the settlement. Primary care is not “minor medicine” — it is the level where a large share of diseases can be prevented or caught in time.

gp.title: General practitioner
gp.text: Managing chronic diseases — hypertension, diabetes —, organising screenings, vaccinations, and the first examination that decides whether specialist care is needed. Where a district is unfilled, all of this is squeezed into a substitute's reduced consulting hours.

ped.title: Paediatrician
ped.text: Age-linked status examinations, the vaccination schedule and monitoring development are the basis of recognising childhood diseases early. Vacancies in paediatric districts affect the youngest — see them on the map with the “paediatric” type filter.

dental.title: Dentist
dental.text: Caries and periodontal disease are preventable, and early detection of oral cancer can save lives — all of which depends on regular dental screening. In a vacant district the population typically only has local access to emergency care: prevention is the first thing to fall away.

eesztInfo.title: How we matched the EESZT data
eesztInfo.subtitle: EESZT download: {asOf} · NEAK data: {month} · every step is traceable
eesztInfo.p1: The map is built on NEAK's monthly vacancy lists and contracted-provider registry; these define the districts and their FIN codes. The EESZT supplement adds no districts. It only attaches further official public data to existing districts: the district number, the licensed premises, on-call participation, public funding, and for filled districts the financed provider. Whatever cannot be linked unambiguously is not shown, and we give the reason.
eesztInfo.regFinszolg: Services financed by NEAK: FIN code (FINKOD), organisational-unit code (NNGYK9_KOD), service type (TIP), official service name (FINNEV), provider name (INEV), institution code (INTKOD) and the first 8 digits of the provider's tax number (ADOIGSZ_8).
eesztInfo.regEuszolg: Register of healthcare providers: provider id (EUSZOLG_AZONOSITO), name, tax number, seat.
eesztInfo.regEngedely: Operating licences: licence id, organisational-unit code (SZERVEZETI_EGYSEG_KOD), provider id, premises address, profession (SZAKMA_KOD), public funding (KOZFINANSZIROZOTT) and on-call participation.
eesztInfo.p2: The link in the first column opens the register on the public EESZT portal. The raw download is archived unchanged in the project repository, so it can be re-run and checked at any time.
eesztInfo.p3a: The EESZT master-data page loads its data from a public REST endpoint. We used the same endpoint, paging with 500 rows per page:
eesztInfo.p3b: Each download checks that the number of rows received exactly matches the total the server reports (totalRowCount), that there are no duplicate rows, and that the total did not change during the download. If any check fails, the download stops with an error and no data is taken over. The download code:
eesztInfo.s1: Starting point: every district in NEAK's latest monthly data (filled, vacant, terminated) with its FIN code.
eesztInfo.s2: FIN code → NEAK_FINSZOLG: looked up in the FINKOD field. Only rows of the branch's own type are used: TIP = FOG for dental, TIP = HSZ for GP. A FIN code can appear in several rows (several organisational units); all of them are kept.
eesztInfo.s3: NEAK_FINSZOLG.NNGYK9_KOD → EUSZOLG_ENGEDELY_PUBLIKUS.SZERVEZETI_EGYSEG_KOD: the unit's operating licences are found by exact match on the unit code.
eesztInfo.s4: Profession filter: only licences for the district's own profession are accepted. GP: 6301 general practice, 6302 paediatric general practice, 6303 mixed general practice. Dental: 1300 dental care, 1304 paediatric dentistry, 1305 school dentistry.
eesztInfo.s5: Choosing the licence: if there are several, we take the one whose premises lie in the district's NEAK settlement and that names an actual address.
eesztInfo.s6: Provider check: the licence's EUSZOLG_AZONOSITO leads to the provider in EUSZOLG_PUBLIKUS, whose tax number (first 8 digits) is compared with NEAK_FINSZOLG.ADOIGSZ_8.
eesztInfo.p4: Every link rests on an exact match of official codes. No name-based or similarity (fuzzy) matching is used anywhere. The matching code:
eesztInfo.c1: if a FIN code belongs to several organisational units whose licences name different addresses, we do not pick one: no premises are shown for that district, and it appears among the unmatched with the reason "ambiguous".
eesztInfo.c2: if the licensed premises lie in another settlement than the district's NEAK seat, the premises are shown but flagged ("differs from the district's NEAK seat"). "Budapest" and "Budapest VIII. kerület" are treated as matching.
eesztInfo.c3: whether the licensee's and the financed provider's tax numbers match is shown in its own column ("Tax number matches").
eesztInfo.c4: the district number and provider name are shown only when every row of a FIN code carries the same value.
eesztInfo.c5: every district falls into exactly one category: it either has a matched licence or a recorded reason why not. The build stops if matched plus unmatched districts do not add up to the total.
eesztInfo.n1: The financed provider name and institution code are shown only for filled districts (the contracted provider NEAK itself publishes).
eesztInfo.n2: For vacant and terminated districts no free-text name field is taken over: organisational-unit names often carry the former physician's name ({n} such vacant districts in the current data; their names are not published).
eesztInfo.n3: Of the trace codes, the provider id is also given only for filled districts; the other codes (organisational unit, licence) carry no personal data.
eesztInfo.n4: The build checks these rules automatically and stops on any violation; tests protect them as well.
eesztInfo.p7: The official service name (FINNEV) is free text, so we extract only the district number, with a strict pattern. For example "Tatabánya 8. sz. gyermek körzet." → "8. gyermek körzet", "BETÖLTETLEN - 1. körzet, Beremend" → "1. körzet". If the pattern is not unambiguous, or the result contains a personal-name marker, no district number is shown.
eesztInfo.p8: Licensed premises addresses are geocoded with OpenStreetMap Nominatim, at most 1 request per second, cached. We first search at street level with the postcode, then without it. If neither returns a result, the settlement centre is used, shown as a fainter point on the map and in the "Approximate location" column. Districts without coordinates are not drawn. eesztInfo.p9: Percentages refer to the total number of districts. The list of unmatched districts, with reasons, is available in the table marked with the warning icon, filterable and exportable.

xc.s1: We take the NEAK records the code chain could not pair with an EESZT licence — districts and services alike.
xc.s2: The NEAK surgery address is normalized (accents folded, abbreviations expanded: u. → utca, krt → körút, house number extracted, Budapest districts unified), and so is every premises address in the licence register. An exact agreement in the record's own profession family is a first-tier hit.
xc.s3: The two registers often spell the same address differently (“Semmelweis I. u. 1.” ↔ “Semmelweis utca 1.”), so a second pass compares the street's stem, its type and the house number, ignoring abbreviated forenames and “Dr.” prefixes. “Kossuth tér” still differs from “Kossuth utca”.
xc.s4: Where the address leads nowhere we use the provider's tax number: the financing register's tax field is matched against the provider register, and we check whether that provider holds a licence of the right profession in the settlement. This is a deterministic link, not a similarity.
xc.s5: Finally the weaker evidence: the same street at another house number, then a provider-name match (legal forms — Kft., Korlátolt Felelősségű Társaság — and generic words removed, from 60% overlap).
xc.c1t: A suggestion is not a pairing
xc.c1: Nothing from the cross-check enters the district data: it never changes a match and never counts towards the coverage numbers. It is a separate table with its own reasoning.
xc.c2: A dental district only matches a dental licence (13xx), a GP district a GP one (63xx). If the address holds only another profession's licence, that is reported as its own result.
xc.c3: A column states whether the hit came from the premises address, the street name or the provider name, and a full sentence explains it.
xc.c4t: The name policy holds here too
xc.c4: Free-text names appear only where NEAK itself publishes a contracted physician; everywhere else the output carries codes, addresses and profession names only.
xc.names: The cross-check follows the same name rules as the rest: the free-text names of organisational units and premises are never exported, because they often carry a physician's name. The suggestions rest on codes, addresses and profession names.
xc.rEesztOnly: Services that exist in EESZT only
xc.p9: Clicking a number lists every candidate row by row (unit, licence id, premises, profession), filterable and exportable.
xc.l1: An address match is not proof: several services can share a building, and a mistyped address can produce an accidental hit.
xc.l2: A provider-name match is the weakest evidence: a rename or a similarly named company can mislead.
xc.l3: The “in EESZT only” list is not necessarily a missing district: it can be an on-call, school or other service the published NEAK lists do not carry.
xc.drillSubtitle: Every candidate row by row — {kind} records
xc.s6: The other direction is checked too: which dental and GP services appear in the EESZT financed-services register while the published NEAK lists do not contain them — those are also compared with the earlier monthly NEAK snapshots.
xc.c5: A health centre can hold ten or twenty surgeries at the same address, so candidates are ranked by strength: the one the provider's tax number confirms comes first, then the exact address match. The table flags the tax agreement in a column of its own.

risk.heading: Vacancy risk
risk.explain: Every {kind} district with a doctor today, ranked by how likely it is to go vacant within {horizon} months. The model learned from the archived monthly NEAK snapshots ({months} complete months since {from}): it measured the actual transition rates behind each characteristic. It is transparent, not a black box — every row states what pushed its own number up or down.
risk.baseRate: the chance that an average {kind} district goes vacant within {horizon} months
risk.checkExplain: The model was fitted on the months before {from} and used to rank what happened afterwards: {events} real vacancies. In the decile it marked riskiest, {top} went vacant against {base} on average — a {lift}× hit rate (AUC {auc}). Good for ranking, not for individual prediction.

risk.countySubtitle: How many districts fall into the two riskiest bands
risk.factorsExplain: The multipliers are not assumptions but rates measured in the archive: how much more (or less) often a district went vacant with that characteristic. The events column is the number of observed vacancies, the last one the raw 12-month rate.
risk.l1: This is a ranking, not a prediction: it says where to look first, not whether a given doctor will leave.
risk.l2: The archived months are unevenly spaced (1–14 months apart), so transitions are converted to monthly exposure.
risk.l3: The model cannot see the physician's age — the most important missing factor; "same physician for X years" only approximates it.
risk.l4: Provider size and neighbouring vacancies are taken from today's state; every other characteristic uses only its own past in each month.

survival.heading: Survival analysis: how long does a vacancy last?
survival.explain: How many districts are vacant today cannot tell a three-month handover from a ten-year hole. The archive can: every monthly snapshot since {from} names the {kind} districts without a physician, so every vacancy can be followed. {spells} vacancy spells in total, {refilled} of which ended with a district being filled again and {open} still running. The curve is a Kaplan–Meier estimate: the share of vacancies still open after N months — spells that are still running are kept as censored rather than dropped.

But a district can serve several settlements: when the seat goes vacant, the villages attached to it appear nowhere in a seat-based count. This section turns the question around and classifies every settlement.

composite.heading: Composite care-risk index
composite.explain: Each analysis answers one question: is there a physician, how far is the next surgery, how old is the population, how likely is a vacancy. Trouble is when they point the same way at once. The index is the weighted mean of eight components, computed for every settlement, and every score can be taken apart into the components that made it.
composite.caveat: This is a comparison, not a verdict: a high index means several public indicators point the same way — not that care is unavailable there. Distances are crow-flies kilometres from the settlement centre, not travel time. Every component enters as a national rank percentile so that kilometres and shares can be added at all.

composite.weightsTitle: What is the index made of?
composite.weightsExplain: The weights are deliberately round numbers and are published here. Where a component has no data for a settlement it is left out of that settlement's mean rather than estimated.

emergency.explain: Until now the site could only say that a district is vacant. The other half is in the same EESZT register it downloads every month: {oncall} central on-call services and {ambulance} ambulance units with a licence and premises. So for every settlement and every district without a physician it can say how far the nearest on-call surgery and ambulance station are.

travel.heading: Driving time instead of straight lines

On an ordinary Wednesday ({day}) scheduled buses leave from {settlements} of {total} settlements — the question is whether any of them goes, without a change, to where the care is.
transit.caveat: "No direct bus" does not mean unreachable: with a change it often works. But a change is exactly what an eighty-year-old cannot always make. Trains are not in the data (MÁV releases its timetable only on request), and Budapest runs on a separate feed, so the capital's districts are left out of this section.

officialmap.explain: The cross-check works out which operating licence a praxis runs under from addresses, tax numbers and names. NEAK's extended financing register (NEAK_FINSZOLG_EXT) simply says: every FIN code carries the provider's six-character id, name and tax number. Here the two sit side by side.

gyse.heading: Medical aids: where can a prescription be filled?
gyse.explain: A prescription is only half the story; the other half is whether there is a place within reach that actually hands over the walking frame, the hearing aid or the orthopaedic shoe. The EESZT retailer register holds {premises} premises of {providers} providers, each with a licence and an address.
gyse.caveat: The seven licensed activities are not interchangeable: a repair workshop does not hand over a walking frame, and an orthopaedic shoemaker does not fit hearing aids. So the distance question is asked about the three that dispense (own shop, branch, own workshop). The register licenses the activity, not the product range — a shop in town does not mean they have your size.

licenceHistory.heading: How old is the unit a district works under?
licenceHistory.explain: The EESZT licence register answers for past dates, so {snapshots} snapshots were taken between {from} and {to}. From those it can be read, district by district, since when the organisational unit it works under today has existed.
licenceHistory.limit: What it does not tell us is who ran the district before. It turns out a unit belongs to its provider permanently — of the 81,600 units present both in January 2024 and in July 2026, exactly two changed provider. A change of operator therefore creates a new unit, and the link between a FIN code and a unit has no public history. The date of a new unit is an upper bound: the present arrangement is no older than that.

privacy.heading: Privacy notice
privacy.lead: This site measures almost nothing, which is why this notice is short and concrete: what is stored, by whom, for how long, and how to say no.

controller.title: Who the controller is
controller.text: The data controller is Dr. Zoltán Dul as a private individual: he built the site and runs it, and every decision about what is processed, why and for how long is his. The praxisterkep.hu domain is registered to Mackó Dental Kft., which provides the domain and the technical background; it does not decide the site's content or its data processing and does not use visitors' data for its own purposes. The site is a private initiative, not a publication of NEAK, OKFŐ, Mackó Dental Kft. or any authority, and serves no commercial purpose: no advertising, nothing sold, no customers gathered. Contact: GitHub @ZoliQua, or as given on dulzoltan.hu.

what.title: What data is processed
what.text: By default none about visitors. No registration, no sign-in, no newsletter, and no visitor data stored in our own systems. What the site does download and archive is public-interest data the authorities have already published — it is not about visitors. The health data shown comes from those public lists; the site holds no patient or other personal health data.

analytics.title: Visitor statistics (only with consent)
analytics.text: The site uses Google Analytics 4 — but only if you explicitly accept it on the bar. Without consent the measurement code is not even loaded and no cookie is set. With consent, Google Analytics stores a random identifier in a cookie and records pages viewed, referrer, approximate location and device type. IP addresses are anonymised, and advertising signals and personalisation are switched off. The same consent starts Vercel Speed Insights: with no cookie and no identifier, it records how fast the page loads and responds, with the device type and the page address. The query part of the address (the county or settlement chosen, for instance) is cut off before sending.

legalBasis.title: Legal basis
legalBasis.text: Your consent (GDPR Art. 6(1)(a)), which you may withdraw at any time without consequence; withdrawal does not affect prior lawfulness.

retention.title: For how long
retention.text: Google Analytics event data is deleted after 14 months. Speed Insights measurements are kept by Vercel under its own retention rules; they carry no identifier. Your choice is kept in your own browser until you clear it.

processors.title: Who else is involved
processors.text: Google Ireland Limited (Analytics, only with consent; Google is certified under the EU–US Data Privacy Framework), Vercel Inc. (hosting, and with consent the Speed Insights measurements), Google Fonts (typefaces), and MapTiler with OpenStreetMap only if you open the street map. Your browser contacts these for technical reasons, which makes your IP address visible to them.

storage.title: What your browser keeps
storage.text: Your language choice, map-layer settings, your last PDF export settings and your cookie decision. These stay on your device and never reach us.

rights.title: Your rights
rights.text: Access, rectification, erasure, restriction, objection, and withdrawal of consent at any time. You may complain to the Hungarian data protection authority (naih.hu) or go to court.

mortality.heading: What does an empty district cost? — avoidable mortality
mortality.lead: Avoidable mortality counts the people who die before 75 of something timely care or prevention should have stopped. In {year} it ranged from {bestValue} ({best}) to {worstValue} ({worst}) per 100,000 — a {times}-fold gap inside one country.
mortality.what: NNGYK follows Eurostat's two lists and sorts causes into three groups that do not overlap. Their sum is avoidable mortality; the bar shows what a typical járás's is made of.
mortality.scatterHeading: Does it go with vacant districts?
mortality.findingRaw: Across the 174 rural járás, the association between the share of vacant GP districts and {what} is {strength}: r = {r} (p {p}, n = {n}).
mortality.findingPartial: It survives holding income constant: partial r = {r} (p {p}) — so it is not only that poorer places have both more empty districts and more deaths.
mortality.findingIncome: Income itself is more strongly associated (r = {r}).
mortality.caveat: This is an association between places, not proof that a given vacancy causes deaths. Vacancy, poverty, ageing and mortality reinforce one another; holding income constant reduces that, it does not remove it. A vacant district is not unserved: a substitute doctor covers it.
mortality.source: Source: NNGYK mortality database, {year}; standardised death rate (SHA) per 100,000, 2013 European Standard Population. GP vacancy from NEAK's monthly lists.
mortality.findingPartial2: Holding education (the share of graduates) constant as well as income leaves partial r = {r} (p {p}): part of the link mirrors poverty and low schooling, but something of it remains beyond them.
mortality.findingPartial2None: Holding education (the share of graduates) constant as well as income, the association is no longer distinguishable from chance: partial r = {r} (p {p}). Poverty and low schooling explain the raw association.

links.heading: What goes with what?
links.lead: The whole picture in one table: rows are five aspects of care, columns the outcomes and circumstances. Each cell is a correlation across the 174 rural járás; click a cell to see its scatter, so no number has to be taken on trust.
links.pairFinding: The association is {strength}: r = {r} (rank correlation: {rho}), {n} járás.
links.caveat: A correlation measures how places move together, not a cause. Anything tied to many variables at once — poverty, ageing — can produce an association where there is no direct link. A result that did not come out is a result too: the share of registered chronic patients, for one, is unrelated to vacancy.

grants.lead: Every year NEAK pays a lump sum to a doctor who takes over a district vacant for at least a year, and supports GPs buying a practice right. NEAK publishes the winners — not what became of the district. We matched every winner's address to a district in NEAK's monthly data and checked whether it has a doctor today.

Matching is by surgery address; where one address hosts several districts and the monthly data cannot tell which one the winner took, it is not counted. Winners' names are not shown.

europe.heading: Where does Hungary stand in Europe?
europe.ratio: In {year}, Hungary had {hu} and the EU-27 average {eu} {what} deaths per 100,000.
europe.nngyk: The national figure from NNGYK's district data for {year} is {value} — the same causes, divided as Eurostat divides them (causes on both lists half to each).
europe.note: The two sources differ in level: NNGYK's figures are some 15% below Eurostat's in both halves, while their all-cause rates agree. The cause list (Eurostat's 2022 list adds COVID-19 as preventable) or the age limit is the likely reason; NNGYK's method note is a PDF. So Eurostat is used for Europe and NNGYK inside the country — never mixed.
europe.source: Source: Eurostat, Treatable and preventable mortality of residents (under 75, 2013 European Standard Population, per 100,000);

outcomeMethod.heading: Outcomes and circumstances — how they are made
outcomeMethod.lead: The mortality, income, labour and population figures on the analysis page come from outside public sources (NNGYK, KSH TIMEA, the KSH census, NFSZ, NEAK), bound by the same rule as the rest of the site: every number traces to an archived source file, and a half-read source fails rather than being published.

mortality.title: Avoidable mortality — NNGYK
mortality.text: The national public-health centre publishes, per járás and county, the standardised death rate (SHA, per 100,000, 2013 European Standard Population) and the standardised mortality ratio (SHH, 100 = what national rates predict). Avoidable mortality follows Eurostat's two lists for deaths under 75; NNGYK sorts causes into three groups that do not overlap — treatable only, preventable only, and both. Their sum is total avoidable mortality, treatable-only plus both is the care-sensitive part; rates on one standard population add up. NNGYK ships each cause as a ~22 MB interactive map; the ~270 KB part carrying the numbers is archived byte for byte with the SHA-256 of the whole original. For the European comparison Eurostat's hlth_cd_apr series for Hungary and the EU-27 are used (source Q). Eurostat splits the causes on both lists half to treatable and half to preventable; NNGYK publishes them as a group of their own, so the NNGYK figures are also given in Eurostat's split (treatable: treatable-only + half of both; preventable: preventable-only + half of both). The levels differ: NNGYK's national 2024 figure is some 15% below Eurostat's 2023 one in both halves while all-cause mortality agrees; the cause-list version or the age limit is the likely reason. The two sources are never mixed.

whyNotKsh.title: Why not KSH's district death table?
whyNotKsh.text: KSH publishes district deaths by cause, age and year too (Statinfo NH3A07), and avoidable mortality could be computed from it. But KSH hides every cell under three for confidentiality and draws it exactly like a zero. Broken down by járás × cause × age × year most cells are that small, so the hidden deaths would vanish — and the small rural járás would look healthiest. NNGYK works from the unmasked microdata.

income.title: Income — KSH TIMEA, NAV data
income.text: Yearly domestic income forming the personal income tax base, per permanent resident, by settlement, járás and county, from KSH's public TIMEA map service. Forints are not comparable across years — inflation ran at 15–25% in 2022–23 — so comparisons over time are always as a share of that year's median járás.

jobs.title: Jobseekers — NFSZ
jobs.text: The National Employment Service publishes settlement figures monthly: registered jobseekers by place of residence on the 20th, and the 15–64 population (KSH, previous 1 January). The share is one over the other. Before 2024 the data is quarterly, back to 2019, so the chart runs on a true time axis. Every sheet must add up to its own printed county total or it is rejected.

population.title: Births, deaths, migration — KSH TIMEA
population.text: Natural change (live births minus deaths) and the domestic migration balance (permanent and temporary moves together), both per 1,000. For járás and settlements the 2022–2025 average is used: the 2020–21 pandemic excess is not to be read as a local trait, and in a small village one event moves the rate by several per thousand.

stats.title: Associations — what is computed
stats.text: Correlations are Pearson's r across the 174 rural járás, with Spearman's rank correlation beside it; p comes from the t-distribution. The partial correlation shows what remains once income differences are taken out: r_xy·z = (r_xy − r_xz·r_yz) / √((1 − r_xz²)(1 − r_yz²)). Scatter lines are least-squares fits to the dots shown, computed by the page, not taken from stored values.

grid.title: The 3 × 3 grid
grid.text: Rural járás are split into thirds by income and by GP vacancy, and each of the nine cells shows the median avoidable mortality. Within a row income is nearly constant: if the numbers rise left to right, mortality is higher where more districts are empty even among equally poor or rich places.

capital.title: Why the capital is left out of the associations
capital.text: KSH TIMEA publishes the capital as one settlement and one járás, so a kerület has no income or migration balance of its own. Kerület appear with their own mortality, jobseeker and vacancy figures; where a number is Budapest's as a whole, the page says so.

cross.title: The four cross-sections
cross.text: No new source, only the settlement profiles: when a district fell vacant from NEAK's monthly lists, the driving time to the nearest staffed surgery on the OpenStreetMap road network, direct buses from the Volánbusz timetable, age structure from the 2022 census, care deserts from the existing cluster analysis. Affected population is not summed here, because one empty district in a town would count the whole town.

limits.title: What these numbers do not say
limits.text: They measure associations between places, not causes and not people: that more avoidable deaths go with more vacancies across járás does not mean a given empty district causes a given death. A vacant district is not unserved — public data does not show substitution. A missing association is a result too: registered chronic patients are unrelated to vacancy.

census.title: Census — KSH, 2022
census.text: From the public database of the 2022 KSH census, by settlement, járás and county (CC BY 4.0). Each measure is one published count over another: graduates per resident 20+ (education is published from age 7, so schoolchildren sit in the lowest bands; a degree before 20 is negligible, which keeps this one share clean), the employed per resident 15+, the digitally inactive per resident 6+, half-comfort, no-comfort and emergency dwellings per occupied dwelling, and households of only the 65+. KSH hides small cells; the measure is then empty, except for dwellings, where the comfort levels add up exactly to the occupied dwellings, so the poor ones can be taken from the total — an identity checked on every complete row. Járás and county values are KSH's own, not sums of settlements. Ethnicity data is deliberately not used.

education.title: Two controls: income and education
education.text: Poor járás are short of income and schooling at once, and each goes with mortality on its own. The main association is therefore also given as a second-order partial correlation: r_xy·zw = (r_xy·z − r_xw·z · r_yw·z) / √((1 − r_xw·z²)(1 − r_yw·z²)), z income, w the share of graduates. GP vacancy and avoidable mortality: r = {raw} raw, {income} with income held still, {both} (p {p}) with both: most of the link is poverty and low schooling, but part of it remains. All three numbers are shown so the reader can see how much rests on the control.

sbo.title: Distance to an emergency department
sbo.text: From NEAK's inpatient list, the sites with a unit of profession 4602 (care organised in an emergency unit) or 4605 (the same for children) — 67 sites. Driving time is made like every other: on the OpenStreetMap road network, free flow, from the settlement centre. A járás's value is the median of its settlements. The raw association with treatable mortality vanishes once income and education are held still — reported as a null result.

grants.title: Settlement and practice-right grants — NEAK
grants.text: NEAK publishes each year's winners of the GP and dental settlement grants and the GP practice-right grant: county, settlement, surgery address (2019, 2021–2025; the 2020 list is not on NEAK's site). Winners' names are neither stored nor shown. Each winner's address is matched to a district (FIN) in NEAK's monthly data: first a district listed vacant at that address in the grant year or the two before; where one address has several, the one that left the vacant list in the grant year or the next; where that does not decide, the winner is marked ambiguous and left out of every share. Obvious slips in NEAK's lists (wrong county, misspelt settlement) are corrected by rule or by a flagged hand correction. Comparison group: districts vacant 12+ months at the end of the year without a grant. The groups do not differ at random — a doctor chose the granted district — so the gap is not the grant's pure effect. On top of this, a matched comparison: each granted district is set against up to five districts without a grant from the month it was itself still vacant, same branch, same vacancy band (12–24 months, 2–5 years, over 5 years) and same settlement-size band (cut at 1,000, 3,000 and 10,000), in the same county where possible; selection is deterministic (nearest vacancy length, then FIN).

forecast.title: Forecast: a year from now
forecast.text: A flow model: vacant in 12 months = vacant now − expected refills + expected new vacancies. Expected new vacancies are the sum of the filled districts' 12-month risk (from the risk model); each vacant district's refill chance is 1 − S(e + 12) / S(e), e the months it has been vacant, S its county's Kaplan–Meier curve (the national one below 60 spells). No refill is assumed beyond the curve's end. The 90% band treats districts as independent, so it is narrower than the true uncertainty. Back-test between two archived months — refills by the same method, new vacancies at the model's base rate, since past per-district risk is not kept (GP: {from} → {to}) — new vacancies {newPred} expected / {newAct} actual, refills {fillPred} / {fillAct}; the forecast leans slightly pessimistic. Not a clean test: the survival curve has seen that period. Per settlement one probability is published: that in 12 months at least one district serving it is vacant, P = 1 − Π(1 − pᵢ) · Π qⱼ, pᵢ the filled districts' risk, qⱼ the vacant ones' refill chance. A GP district counts for every settlement it serves, a dental one for its seat. The chance is said of the settlement, never of a named doctor's district.

notAvailable.title: What is missing, because no public data exists
notAvailable.text: We wanted to set screening participation (breast, cervical, colorectal) and vaccination coverage beside vacancy — the measurable part of prevention. No institution publishes them by járás or settlement in a public, machine-readable form: we went through NNGYK's whole public file list and the NEAK and KSH sites. No estimate is published; when the data becomes public, it goes in.

europe.heading: Europe: where does Hungarian primary care stand?
europe.lead: The questions the site asks of a district — is there a doctor, does the patient get to one, what does care achieve, what does it cost — asked of the 27 member states of the European Union and the United Kingdom, from the joint data collection of Eurostat and the OECD, and finally of the regions on either side of the border. Choose above which countries to compare and which one to put in focus; the bar at the top switches between the GP and the dental measures.

overview.heading: {country} among the countries chosen
overview.lead: Eight headline measures, each at its latest year. A card's colour shows which third of the ranking of the countries chosen the country in focus falls into; the dots are the other countries, the tick is the EU-27. A card takes you to its section.
overview.hint: Click a dot to put that country in focus across the page. The ranking uses comparable years only: a figure more than five years older than the newest one is shown but not ranked.

workforce.heading: Who is in the surgery?
workforce.lead: How many doctors there are for the population, how many of them are GPs, how many are close to retiring, and how many are coming after them. The figures count practising doctors — those actually seeing patients — not everyone on the register.

access.heading: Do patients get to a doctor?
access.lead: Two kinds of question from two sources: how many people saw a doctor in the past year (the European Health Interview Survey, EHIS), and how many say they needed to but did not get there (the EU-SILC household survey). Both are people's own answers, not registers.

outcomes.heading: What does care achieve?
outcomes.lead: What depends on primary care: deaths that timely treatment or prevention would have avoided, the reach of organised screening, flu vaccination of the old, and hospital admissions that good GP care would make unnecessary (OECD).

spending.heading: What do we spend on it?
spending.lead: Health spending per inhabitant in purchasing power, how much of it goes to medical and dental practices and to prevention — and how much patients pay out of their own pocket.

pay.heading: What do doctors earn?
pay.lead: The OECD gives earnings as a multiple of each country's average wage, so countries with different price levels can be compared. Salaried and self-employed doctors are shown separately, because the two are not the same income.

needs.heading: Who needs care?
needs.lead: Before counting doctors: how old and how ill is the population to be cared for. Where life is shorter, fewer years are lived in health and long-standing illness is more common, more primary care is needed, not less.

gpDensity.name: General practitioners
gpDensity.note: Countries do not count GPs alike: in Poland many family doctors are filed among other generalists, in Portugal every generalist is included. All generalist doctors are therefore shown as well.

generalistDensity.name: All generalist doctors
generalistDensity.explain: GPs and other non-specialist doctors together, per 100,000 inhabitants. This wider circle evens out the countries' different filing.

dentistDensity.name: Dentists
dentistDensity.note: Only practising dentists are shown. Where a country reports only professionally active or licensed dentists (Slovakia since 2004), the cell is empty: the concepts do not mix.

physicianDensity.name: All doctors
physicianDensity.explain: All practising doctors, specialists included, per 100,000 inhabitants.

nurseDensity.name: Nurses
nurseDensity.explain: Practising nurses per 100,000 inhabitants. Where primary care is short of doctors, much of the work falls to them.

physicians55.name: Doctors aged 55 or over
physicians55.explain: The share of doctors aged 55 or over: those who may retire within ten years.
physicians55.note: The share is computed from the published age bands by an exact identity: the three older bands, or where an older band is missing, the total less the three younger ones. If neither is complete, there is no value. It covers all doctors, not GPs only.

medGraduates.name: Medical graduates
medGraduates.explain: Doctors graduating in the year, per 100,000 inhabitants.
medGraduates.note: Graduates include foreign students. Romania, Bulgaria and Hungary have many, and most return home.

dentGraduates.name: Dental graduates
dentGraduates.explain: Dentists graduating in the year, per 100,000 inhabitants.
dentGraduates.note: Graduates include foreign students, most of whom return home.

gpVisit.name: Saw a GP in the past year
gpVisit.explain: The share of people aged 15 or over who saw a general practitioner in the past 12 months (EHIS, 2019).
gpVisit.pairName: Saw a GP: city and countryside
gpVisit.pairExplain: The same question among those living in cities (densely populated areas) and in rural, thinly populated areas. Rows are sorted by the gap between the two.

dentVisit.name: Saw a dentist in the past year
dentVisit.explain: The share of people aged 15 or over who saw a dentist in the past 12 months (EHIS, 2019; the United Kingdom 2014).
dentVisit.pairName: Saw a dentist: city and countryside
dentVisit.pairExplain: The same question among those living in cities and in rural, thinly populated areas. Rows are sorted by the gap between the two.

consultations.name: Doctor consultations
consultations.explain: Doctor consultations (GPs and specialists together) per inhabitant per year, from the practices' own records.
consultations.note: This has no good direction: many consultations can mean good access, or patients returning for a prescription or a referral.

dentConsultations.name: Dental consultations
dentConsultations.explain: Dental consultations per inhabitant per year.

unmetMed.name: Needed a doctor but did not get there
unmetMed.explain: The share of people aged 16 or over who needed a medical examination in the past year but did not get one because it was too expensive, too far, or the waiting list too long (EU-SILC).
unmetMed.note: Self-reported: people used to having no doctor less often feel they missed one. Hungary's figure is therefore lower than the visits would suggest, and is no proof of good access on its own.
unmetMed.pairName: Unmet medical need: poor and rich
unmetMed.pairExplain: The same question in the poorest and the richest income fifth. Rows are sorted by the gap between the two.

unmetDent.name: Needed a dentist but did not get there
unmetDent.explain: The share of people aged 16 or over who needed a dental examination but did not get one for cost, distance or a waiting list (EU-SILC).
unmetDent.note: Self-reported, with the same weakness as the medical question: people who do not go to a dentist often do not feel the lack.
unmetDent.pairName: Unmet dental need: poor and rich
unmetDent.pairExplain: The same question in the poorest and the richest income fifth. Rows are sorted by the gap between the two.

avoidable.name: Avoidable mortality
avoidable.explain: Deaths under 75 from causes that timely care or prevention would have avoided, standardised to the 2013 European Standard Population, per 100,000 inhabitants (Eurostat).
avoidable.note: Inside Hungary, by district, the site uses NNGYK's figures, whose level is lower; the two are never mixed (see the methodology).

treatable.name: Treatable mortality
treatable.explain: The part of avoidable mortality that depends on health care: deaths timely, effective treatment could have prevented.

preventable.name: Preventable mortality
preventable.explain: The part of avoidable mortality that depends on prevention: tobacco, alcohol, accidents, vaccine-preventable disease.

screenBreast.name: Breast screening
screenBreast.explain: The share of women in the target age group screened in the organised breast-screening programme (programme data, not a survey).
screenBreast.note: Programme data: it shows who reached the organised screening. Women screened privately are not in it, and how many there are differs by country.

screenCervical.name: Cervical screening
screenCervical.explain: The share of women in the target age group screened in the organised cervical-screening programme (programme data).
screenCervical.note: Programme data: smears taken privately or as part of a gynaecological visit are not in it, so in some countries the true share may be higher.

screenColorectal.name: Colorectal screening
screenColorectal.explain: The share of the target age group taking part in the organised colorectal-screening programme (programme data).

flu65.name: Flu vaccination, 65 and over
flu65.explain: The share of people aged 65 or over vaccinated against influenza. The shot is usually given by the GP.

admAsthmaCopd.name: Avoidable admissions: asthma and COPD
admAsthmaCopd.explain: Hospital admissions for asthma or chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, per 100,000 inhabitants aged 15 or over, age- and sex-standardised (OECD). With good GP care most are avoidable.
admAsthmaCopd.note: An OECD quality indicator; Bulgaria is not an OECD member and is missing. Hospital coding differs between countries.

admHeartFailure.name: Avoidable admissions: heart failure
admHeartFailure.explain: Hospital admissions for congestive heart failure, per 100,000 inhabitants aged 15 or over, standardised (OECD).
admHeartFailure.note: For Hungary only an old figure is available; the page shows it but does not rank it.

admDiabetes.name: Avoidable admissions: diabetes
admDiabetes.explain: Hospital admissions for diabetes, per 100,000 inhabitants aged 15 or over, standardised (OECD).

spendingPps.name: Health spending per inhabitant
spendingPps.explain: Current health expenditure per inhabitant in purchasing power standards (PPS), so that countries with different price levels can be compared.

outOfPocket.name: Paid out of patients' own pockets
outOfPocket.explain: The part of current health spending households pay directly — for medicines, co-payments or private consultations, for instance.

medicalPractices.name: Spending on medical practices
medicalPractices.explain: The share of current health spending that goes to medical practices (GP and outpatient specialist practices).
medicalPractices.note: Whether a consultation happens in a practice or a hospital outpatient department differs by country, so this has no good direction.

dentalPractices.name: Spending on dental practices
dentalPractices.explain: The share of current health spending that goes to dental practices, public and private together.

prevention.name: Spending on prevention
prevention.explain: The share of current health spending that goes to prevention (vaccination, screening, health promotion).

payGpSalaried.name: Pay of salaried GPs
payGpSalaried.explain: Average yearly earnings of salaried GPs as a multiple of the country's average wage (OECD).
payGpSalaried.note: Most Hungarian GPs are self-employed, but the OECD reports the salaried figure for Hungary; this is therefore not what a typical Hungarian GP earns.

payGpSelf.name: Pay of self-employed GPs
payGpSelf.explain: Average yearly earnings of self-employed GPs as a multiple of the average wage (OECD). There is no figure for Hungary.

paySpecSalaried.name: Pay of salaried specialists
paySpecSalaried.explain: Average yearly earnings of salaried specialists as a multiple of the average wage (OECD) — the yardstick for the GP figure: what a doctor gives up by becoming a GP.

payNurse.name: Pay of hospital nurses
payNurse.explain: Average yearly earnings of hospital nurses as a multiple of the average wage (OECD).

share65.name: People aged 65 and over
share65.explain: The share of the population aged 65 or over, on 1 January. The old account for much of a GP's work.
share65.note: This has no good direction: a higher share means more need, not worse care.

lifeExpectancy.name: Life expectancy at birth
lifeExpectancy.explain: How many years a child born now would live on average if the country's present mortality held throughout its life.

healthyYears65.name: Healthy life years at 65
healthyYears65.explain: How many more years a 65-year-old can expect to live without a health problem that limits activity (from the EU-SILC question and mortality).

goodHealth.name: Rate their health as good
goodHealth.explain: The share of people aged 16 or over who rate their health as good or very good (EU-SILC).

longIllness.name: Live with a long-standing illness
longIllness.explain: The share of people aged 16 or over with a long-standing (at least six months) illness or health problem (EU-SILC).
longIllness.note: Self-reported: where more patients are under care, more people know of their illness, so a higher share may partly mean better diagnosis.

vaccDtp.name: Childhood vaccination: diphtheria, tetanus, pertussis
vaccDtp.explain: The share of one-year-olds who received the full primary series (OECD). In Hungary vaccination is organised by the paediatric GP and the health visitor.
vaccDtp.note: Countries measure it differently (registers or surveys, different ages), so small differences are not meaningful.

vaccMeasles.name: Childhood vaccination: measles
vaccMeasles.explain: The share of children vaccinated against measles by the required age (OECD).
vaccMeasles.note: Countries measure it differently, so small differences are not meaningful.

foreignTrained.name: Foreign-trained doctors
foreignTrained.explain: The share of doctors who trained abroad (OECD). It counts the place of the degree, not nationality.
foreignTrained.note: This has no good direction: foreign-trained doctors can fill a gap, or show that a country does not train enough.

scatter.heading: Two measures side by side
scatter.lead: Pick any two measures; each dot is a country at its latest figure. The two dashed lines are the medians of the countries chosen, splitting the field into four quarters.
scatter.note: {n} countries are shown. With so few, no correlation is computed: leaving one or two countries in or out could turn it round. The chart shows where a country stands, not what goes with what.
scatter.tooFew: Too few countries have figures for these two measures.

regions.heading: Map of the regions
regions.lead: Eurostat publishes a few measures for regions (NUTS 2) too: the number of doctors, standardised mortality, life expectancy at birth and GDP per head. Hungary's eight regions can thus be seen among the regions of the countries chosen. Click a region to highlight it.
regions.aria: Map of Europe's regions by the measure chosen
regions.unmapped: {n} regions are in the list but not on the map: overseas territories, or regions whose code was retired in the 2024 classification.

physicians.name: Doctors in the region
physicians.explain: Doctors working in the region per 100,000 inhabitants, all specialties together (there is no GP breakdown at regional level).
physicians.note: Doctors are counted where they work: regions with university and county hospitals stand out, which does not mean the villages there have more doctors.

deathRate.name: Standardised mortality
deathRate.explain: All deaths in the region with differences in age structure removed, per 100,000 inhabitants.
deathRate.note: The latest regional year is 2021, the year of the COVID-19 pandemic, which also shapes the differences between regions.

lifeExpectancy.name: Life expectancy at birth
lifeExpectancy.explain: How many years a child born now would live on average if the region's present mortality held throughout its life.

gdpPps.name: GDP per head
gdpPps.explain: The region's GDP per head in purchasing power, as a percentage of the EU average (EU = 100). A yardstick: richer regions can be expected to have more doctors and better health; the question is whether Hungary's regions do better or worse than that.

border.heading: Across the border
border.lead: Hungary's border regions beside the region facing them in the neighbouring country. Most things are shared here — landscape, climate, often history and language — so more of the difference comes down to care and prosperity. The better value is marked in green.
border.note: The year is given beside each row; where the two regions report different years, both are there. The pairs follow the border from the north, clockwise.

method.title: How is it made?
method.text: The sources, the concepts, and why Eurostat and OECD figures are never mixed.

method.heading: The European comparison
method.lead: How the Europe page is made, and what it cannot say.

sources.title: Sources
sources.text: Eurostat's health and regional databases (source Q) and OECD Health Statistics (source R, CC BY 4.0). Both draw on the same joint OECD–Eurostat–WHO data collection; the OECD is used for three things Eurostat does not publish: avoidable hospital admissions, doctors' pay, and the United Kingdom after 2019. Region outlines are GISCO's NUTS 2024 classification (© EuroGeographics for the administrative boundaries). Every downloaded answer is archived with its date.

oneSource.title: One country, one source
oneSource.text: A country's whole series for a measure comes from one publisher. The United Kingdom's workforce figures are taken from the OECD, but only after the two publishers have been checked to agree on the years they share; if they differ, the build stops. Such a country carries an OECD mark in the ranking.

concepts.title: Measuring the same thing
concepts.text: Practising, professionally active and licensed doctors are three different numbers; practising is shown everywhere, and where a country reports only the other two, the cell is left empty. The share of doctors aged 55 or over is computed from the published age bands by an exact identity, without estimation.

years.title: Every value with its own year
years.text: Each country is shown at its latest published year, with the year beside it. A figure more than five years older than the newest one for the measure is shown but not ranked. The latest published wave of the surveys (EHIS) is 2019.

selfReport.title: Survey and register
selfReport.text: Doctor visits and unmet need are people's own answers. Unmet need has a known weakness: people used to going without say so less often, so it is to be read beside the visits, not instead of them. Screening rates are programme data: tests outside the organised programme are not in them.

regions.title: Regions
regions.text: Only a few measures exist at regional (NUTS 2) level; there is no GP breakdown and no avoidable mortality. Doctors are counted at their workplace, so regions with hospital centres stand out. The border pairs are set by geography, not by the data.

limits.title: What it does not say
limits.text: No correlation is computed from nine or twenty-eight countries, and no measure is claimed to cause another: the page compares, it does not model. Health systems are organised differently (who is the gatekeeper, what counts as a practice), so part of a difference in a measure is a difference in filing.

migration.title: Doctors on the move
migration.text: The OECD health workforce migration table (source R) counts, from the receiving countries' reports, how many doctors work there with a foreign degree and where they got it. Outflow is therefore visible only in reporting countries; their years differ, and place of training is not nationality — graduates who studied abroad as foreign students and went home look like emigrants in the table. No net loss is computed.

change.missing: No figure from ten years earlier (±2 years): {list}

profile.explain: Every rankable measure on one row: right of the centre line where it stands in the better half of the countries chosen, left where it stands in the worse. The length shows how far.

migration.heading: Where do doctors come from and go? — {country}
migration.lead: The OECD counts doctors by where they trained: who works in a country with a foreign degree, and how many doctors trained in a country work in the countries that report it.
migration.splitTitle: Doctors trained at home and abroad
migration.inSummary: {year}: {n} doctors work with a foreign degree, {share} of all doctors. Where they trained:
migration.outSummary: {places} countries report {n} doctors trained here in all (each at its own latest year). At home, {home} home-trained doctors work.
migration.noIn: There are no figures for this country.

migration.mapAria: Map of Europe: how many doctors trained here work in each country
migration.note: Place of training is not nationality. A country that teaches many foreign students sends many doctors home on paper: most of those trained in Hungary who work in Israel, Norway, Sweden, Greece or Cyprus were probably born there and went home. This table cannot separate emigration, so no net loss is computed from it. Only reporting countries appear, each at its own year.

notes.data: The figures come from NEAK’s monthly published lists and the public sources below, as processed each month by Praxis Map. NEAK’s data are for information.
notes.vacant: Vacant ≠ unserved: the residents of a vacant district are usually seen by a substitute doctor. Substitution does not show in the public data, so this report does not claim that any place is without care.
notes.names: A doctor's name appears only for a filled district, where NEAK itself publishes it; never for a vacant or dissolved one.
notes.settlement: The settlement's districts are, in NEAK's registry, those whose catchment lists the settlement; one district may serve several settlements.
notes.sources: Sources: NEAK (vacant services, contracted providers), OKFŐ, EESZT, KSH (gazetteer, 2022 census, TIMEA), NNGYK, NFSZ, Volánbusz timetable (GTFS), OpenStreetMap (ODbL), Government Decrees 290/2014 and 105/2015. The full source list and the method: praxisterkep.hu/modszertan.html.
